spatial_entity.notes: Research slice begins at 318 BCE because that is the earliest continuous Cliopatria Mauryan geometry currently resolved in the atlas.

claim.summary: The best-supported synthesis is that slavery or slave-status relations existed in Mauryan-period India, but differed materially from Greek chattel-slavery expectations and are not shown to have formed the basis of the Mauryan economy. Megasthenes' transmitted statement that Indians did not use slaves is preserved as important contemporary counterevidence, but specialist scholarship and Indian textual evidence treat that statement as insufficient to negate the institution. The atlas therefore records a positive but deliberately low-intensity classification rather than an unresolved yes/no dispute.

territorial_practice.notes: P2 reflects repeated textual/legal attestations and specialist synthesis supporting an established institution while avoiding a claim of economy-wide structural dominance. Megasthenes remains attached as challenging evidence because his Greek category frame and the later transmission of the Indica materially qualify how Mauryan servile statuses should be mapped to slavery.

source.title: Ancient India as Described by Megasthenes and Arrian — Megasthenes fragment on slavery
source.author_or_institution: Megasthenes, transmitted by later Greek authors; J. W. McCrindle translation
source.independence_notes: External Greek ethnographic testimony transmitted through later classical authors.
source.reliability_limitations: The original Indica is lost; the statement survives in later quotations and may reflect Greek categories that did not map cleanly onto Indian status relations.

evidence.evidence_role: contemporary/near-contemporary counterevidence to the slavery classification

source.independence_notes: Specialist legal-historical review explicitly centered on the contradiction between Megasthenes and Indian textual evidence.
source.reliability_limitations: Published in 1963 and dependent on then-current textual scholarship; retained because it directly analyzes the apparent contradiction rather than treating the source traditions mechanically.

source.title: Hindus Beyond the Hindu Kush: Indians in the Central Asian Slave Trade
source.independence_notes: Independent historical synthesis stating that institutionalized slavery was established in India by the beginning of the common era and that earlier evidence points back at least to the Buddha's lifetime.
source.reliability_limitations: Ancient India is contextual background rather than the article's principal empirical focus, so it supports institutional existence and chronology rather than a Mauryan prevalence estimate.
